```{python}
#| echo: false
import json
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

T = Path("../results/tables")
S = json.loads((T / "site_settings.json").read_text("utf-8"))
RUN = "run1"
reg = pd.read_csv(T / RUN / "registered_tests.csv")
bes = pd.read_csv(T / RUN / "reported_beside.csv")
val = pd.read_csv(T / RUN / "validation.csv")
fire = pd.read_csv(T / "fire_region_year.csv")
prov = json.loads((T / RUN / "registered_tests.csv.provenance.json").read_text("utf-8"))


def num(x, d=2):
    """Signed number with a true minus sign."""
    return f"{'−' if x < 0 else '+' if x > 0 else ''}{abs(x):.{d}f}"


def pick(test, region, kind=None):
    t = reg if kind is None else bes[bes["run_kind"] == kind]
    r = t[(t["test"] == test) & (t["region"] == region)]
    assert len(r) == 1, (test, region, kind, len(r))
    return r.iloc[0]


def est(test, region, d=2, kind=None):
    r = pick(test, region, kind)
    return f"{num(r['estimate'], d)} (95% CI {num(r['ci_low'], d)} to {num(r['ci_high'], d)})"


def pc(test, region, kind=None):
    r = pick(test, region, kind)
    return f"{num(r['pct_change'], 0)}% (95% CI {num(r['pct_low'], 0)}% to {num(r['pct_high'], 0)}%)"


def pv(test, region, col="p", kind=None):
    x = pick(test, region, kind)[col]
    return "<0.001" if x < 0.001 else f"{x:.3f}"


def size(test, region):
    return f"{100 * pick(test, region)['size']:.1f}%"


MN = pd.read_csv(T / "methods_numbers.csv", dtype={"group": str})


def mn(measure, group="all", col="value"):
    """One measured number from methods_numbers.csv."""
    r = MN[(MN["measure"] == measure) & (MN["group"] == group)]
    assert len(r) == 1, (measure, group, len(r))
    return r.iloc[0][col]


def mn_range(measure, d=2, pct=False):
    """Lowest to highest value of a measure across its groups."""
    v = MN.loc[MN["measure"] == measure, "value"]
    assert len(v), measure
    tail = "%" if pct else ""
    return f"{v.min():.{d}f}{tail} to {v.max():.{d}f}{tail}"


_park = MN[MN["measure"] == "cnfdb_park_area"].assign(year=lambda t: t["group"].astype(int))
_empty = _park.loc[_park["value"] == 0, "year"]
park_gap_years = f"{_empty.min()} to {_empty.max()}"
assert len(_empty) == _empty.max() - _empty.min() + 1, "the park gap is not one run of years"

n_tests = len(reg)
n_families = reg["family"].nunique()
n_sig = int((reg["significant"] == True).sum())
n_raw = int((reg["p"] < S["alpha"]).sum())
n_seasons = len(fire)
n_winters = int(pick("H1", "PNW")["n"])
n_nino_winters = int(pick("H1", "PNW")["n_group"])
n_nino_seasons = int(pick("H2", "PNW")["n_group"])
pnw = fire[fire["region"] == "PNW"]
n_strong_seasons = int((pnw["strong"] & (pnw["phase"] == "el_nino")).sum())
n_zero = int(fire["zero_fire"].sum())
fwd = val[val["method"] == "expanding window"]
h3a_skill = fwd[fwd["model"] == "H3a"]["skill"]
swe_skill = fwd[fwd["model"] == "H6_swe"]["skill"]
loyo = val[(val["method"] == "leave-one-year-out") & (val["model"] == "H3a")]["coverage"]
fwd_cov = fwd[fwd["model"] == "H3a"]["coverage"]
sizes = reg["size"].dropna()
n_fire_years = int(pick("H3a", "PNW")["n"])
h2_ab = pick("H2", "AB")
fam = reg.groupby("family").size()
zero_rows = fire[fire["zero_fire"]]
us_last = S["fire_last_year_by_region"]["PNW"]
ca_last = S["fire_last_year_by_region"]["BC"]
```

## In short

I asked whether the winter before a fire season tells us anything about how
much burns, and whether El Niño is the useful part of that winter. I fixed
`{python} n_tests` tests in writing before opening any fire data, then ran
them once. After correcting for the number of tests,
`{python} n_sig` of `{python} n_tests` are significant. None of those
`{python} n_sig` links El Niño itself to burned area. What does show up is
the step after it: a wet or snowy winter goes with less burned area that
year in Alberta and Northern California, and in Northern California a wet
winter goes with more burned area the year after. These are associations
over about `{python} n_fire_years` seasons, not causes.

## Method

### The question, and why it is split in two

One El Niño is thought to reach a fire season by two routes. In the north
(the Pacific Northwest, British Columbia and Alberta) the winter runs warmer
and drier, the snowpack is thinner, and the forest dries out earlier. In
Southern California the winter runs wetter, grass grows, and that grass is
fuel once it cures. So I test the chain in pieces: El Niño to winter
weather, winter weather to burned area, and El Niño to burned area directly.

### Regions and years

Seven regions: the Pacific Northwest (Washington, Oregon, Idaho), British
Columbia, Alberta, Alaska, Yukon, and California split at `{python} S["ca_split_lat"]`°N into
Northern and Southern California. Alaska and Yukon were added partway
through and form their own group in the tests. Each region is a whole state,
province or territory, so wet coasts that rarely burn sit inside the climate
averages (see the limitations).

Climate runs from `{python} S["climate_first_year"]` to 2026, which gives
`{python} n_winters` winters. Fire runs from `{python} S["fire_first_year"]`
to `{python} us_last` in the US regions and to `{python} ca_last` in the
Canadian ones, where the fire polygons end: `{python} n_seasons`
region-seasons in all. I analyse every year. El Niño years are compared with
all the others, never studied alone.

A year label means the same thing everywhere: year Y is the winter from
December Y−1 to February Y, the snowpack on 1 April Y, and the fire season
of Y. The 1997-98 El Niño is year 1998.

### What is measured

- **El Niño.** NOAA's relative Oceanic Niño Index (`{python} S["enso_index"]`)
  for December to February. It is the sea-surface temperature anomaly in the
  central Pacific minus the warming of the whole tropical belt, so 1950 and
  2026 are judged on one scale. A winter at or above
  `{python} S["el_nino_threshold"]` °C is an El Niño winter
  (`{python} n_nino_winters` of `{python} n_winters`; `{python} n_nino_seasons`
  in the fire record), and at or above `{python} S["strong_threshold"]` °C a
  strong one (`{python} n_strong_seasons` in the fire record). Every test
  that uses the index is repeated with the older
  `{python} S["enso_robustness_index"]`.
- **Winter weather and snow.** ERA5-Land, a reanalysis: a land model driven
  by observation-corrected weather on a grid of about 9 km. It is a model
  estimate, not a gauge. From it I take December to February precipitation,
  October to March precipitation as a standard score against
  `{python} S["precip_anom_normal_years"][0]`-`{python} S["precip_anom_normal_years"][1]`,
  the snowpack (snow water equivalent) on 1 April as a standard score,
  June to August temperature, and SPEI-3, a drought index that sets three
  months of precipitation against how much water the air could draw.
  Regional means weight each grid cell by its area.
- **Burned area.** Hectares burned in each region's fire season by fires of
  `{python} S["min_fire_ha"]` ha or more. US regions use MTBS, satellite-mapped
  burn boundaries, for ignitions before `{python} S["mtbs_wfigs_cutover"][:4]`,
  and WFIGS incident perimeters from then on, because MTBS mapping lags by
  about two years. Canadian regions use the Canadian National Fire Database
  (CNFDB). I measure area myself in an equal-area projection and do not use
  the sources' own area fields. The tests use the natural log of burned
  area, so a slope reads as a percent change.

The flowchart shows how these are joined.

### Tests fixed before the data

I wrote the hypotheses, the test for each, its direction and how the
p-values would be corrected, and froze that plan on
`{python} S["plan_frozen_date"]` (commit `{python} S["plan_frozen_commit"]`)
before downloading any fire data. Pre-registering matters here because a
record of `{python} n_fire_years` seasons can be made to say almost anything if the tests are
chosen after looking. Changes after the freeze are logged in the plan with
what had been seen at the time; four fire-record rules changed that way,
which is why every burned-area test is also run under the rules as frozen.

| Test | Hypothesis as registered | How it is tested |
|---|---|---|
| H1 | Winter precipitation differs in El Niño winters vs the rest | Difference in means after removing each region's trend; permutation test, bootstrap interval |
| H2 | Fire-season burned area differs after El Niño winters vs the rest | The same, on log burned area |
| H3a | Total effect: ENSO strength predicts burned area, controlling for the long-term trend only | Regression of log burned area on the winter index and year |
| H3b | Direct effect: ENSO strength still predicts burned area after also controlling for summer temperature | H3a with June to August temperature added |
| H4 | El Niño's effect on burned area differs between northern regions and SoCal | One pooled model; the mean northern slope minus Southern California's |
| H5 | Wet years raise burned area afterwards (whiplash mechanism) | Regression on October to March precipitation of the same year and the year before |
| H6 | Low April 1 snowpack and a dry winter predict more burned area | Regressions on the snowpack score and on winter SPEI-3 |
| C1, C2 | Secondary: El Niño's effect on snowpack, and on burned area, changes over time | Regression with an El Niño × year term |

Each test has a registered direction. Where the direction was predicted (for
example, more burned area in the north after El Niño), the test is
one-sided: only a result in that direction can count, and a result the other
way gets a p-value above 0.5. Everything else is two-sided. Confidence
intervals are always two-sided.

### How the tests work

- **Permutation test (H1, H2).** Shuffle which years carry the El Niño
  label `{python} f"{S['n_permutations']:,}"` times and count how often the
  shuffled difference is at least as large as the real one. It assumes
  nothing about the shape of the data.
- **Regression with Newey-West errors (H3, H5, H6, C1, C2).** Ordinary least
  squares, with standard errors that allow a season to resemble the
  `{python} S["hac_maxlags"]` before it. A year term takes out the long-term
  trend, so a region that simply burns more each decade does not pass for an
  El Niño effect.
- **Pooled contrast (H4).** Five regions in one model with errors that allow
  regions to move together within a year (Driscoll-Kraay), tested as one
  number.
- **Correction for many tests.** Within each hypothesis I use the Holm
  correction, which holds the chance of even one false positive in that
  family of tests to `{python} f"{100 * S['alpha']:.0f}"`%. There are
  `{python} n_families` families. I also show the more lenient
  Benjamini-Hochberg figure; a result that passes it but not Holm is
  suggestive at most.
- **Prediction checks.** Each model predicts every season it has not seen,
  two ways: leaving one year out, and fitting only on earlier seasons
  (from `{python} S["forward_min_train_years"]` seasons on). I report how
  often the `{python} S["prediction_level_pct"]`% prediction interval held
  the real value, and whether the model beat a model with the year trend
  alone.

<!-- D96, item 1 of 3. Approved by the owner 2026-10-13. -->

### Why regression, not a trained model

I used regression (a straight-line fit of burned area on a few named
inputs), not a trained machine-learning model. A trained model can pick up
patterns a straight line misses, and with thousands of cases I would have
tried one. Here each region has `{python} n_fire_years` fire seasons. Say a model
with twenty adjustable parts is fitted to those seasons: it can match the
past closely and still say nothing about 2027. A regression has one slope
per question, so I could write each test down before opening the fire data,
and a reader can check it. What this leaves out: effects that are not
straight lines, and inputs that only matter together.

### What the run did

The run checked that the working tree was clean, that every input file
matched its recorded checksum, and that the frozen plan text was
unchanged. It then computed all `{python} n_tests` tests and the runs
reported beside them in one pass and wrote the tables once. The result
files are never edited. If a bug is found, the fix is logged as decided
after results were seen, the rerun goes in a new folder, and both sets of
numbers are shown.

I explored the climate data in three Jupyter notebooks: the winter
precipitation, the drought index and snowpack, and the snow stations. The
notebooks call the same functions as the scripts, so each figure has one
copy of its code, and every figure and table on this site can be rebuilt
without opening a notebook. No registered test ran in a notebook. The tests
ran once, from a script, after a check that the inputs and the plan were
unchanged.

## What the tests found

Effect sizes first. Slopes on burned area are in log points; the percent is
the same slope read as a change in burned area.

- **El Niño and winter precipitation (H1).** Southern California is wetter
  in El Niño winters by `{python} est("H1", "SoCal", 0)` mm, and that
  survives correction (Holm p `{python} pv("H1", "SoCal", "p_holm")`). This
  one is a check, not a finding: I had seen these values before the freeze.
  In the north only Alberta is clearly drier,
  `{python} est("H1", "AB", 0)` mm, and that does not survive correction
  (Holm p `{python} pv("H1", "AB", "p_holm")`).
- **El Niño and burned area (H2, H3a, H3b, H4).** No test is significant in
  any region, before or after correction. The H3a slope per 1 °C of the index
  is `{python} est("H3a", "PNW")` in the Pacific Northwest,
  `{python} est("H3a", "BC")` in British Columbia,
  `{python} est("H3a", "AB")` in Alberta and
  `{python} est("H3a", "SoCal")` in Southern California. The north minus
  Southern California contrast is
  `{python} est("H4", "PNW/BC/AB minus SoCal")`.
- **Wet winters (H5).** In Alberta a winter one standard deviation wetter
  goes with `{python} pc("H5_lag0", "AB")` burned area that year (Holm p
  `{python} pv("H5_lag0", "AB", "p_holm")`). In Northern California it goes
  with `{python} pc("H5_lag1", "NorCal")` the following year (Holm p
  `{python} pv("H5_lag1", "NorCal", "p_holm")`). In Southern California,
  where I expected the next-year effect to be strongest, the slope is
  `{python} est("H5_lag1", "SoCal")` and not significant.
- **Snowpack and winter drought (H6).** All eight slopes outside Southern
  California are negative, the predicted direction. One survives correction:
  Northern California, `{python} pc("H6_swe", "NorCal")` per standard
  deviation of snowpack (Holm p `{python} pv("H6_swe", "NorCal", "p_holm")`).
  Alberta's snowpack slope, `{python} est("H6_swe", "AB")`, passes the
  lenient correction but not Holm (p `{python} pv("H6_swe", "AB", "p_holm")`).
- **Change over time (C1, C2).** None of the `{python} int(fam["C1"] + fam["C2"])` tests is significant.

Before any correction, `{python} n_raw` of `{python} n_tests` tests fall
under p `{python} S["alpha"]`. They are not `{python} n_raw` separate
signals: Alberta accounts for several of them, and snowpack and winter SPEI
measure much the same thing.

## Every test, including nulls

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
ALT = {"greater": "> 0", "less": "< 0", "two-sided": "≠ 0"}
lines = ["| Test | Region | Predicted | Estimate | 95% CI | Change | p | Holm p | After Holm |",
         "|---|---|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---|"]
for _, r in reg.iterrows():
    d = 1 if r["test"] == "H1" else 4 if r["test"] in ("C1", "C2") else 2
    change = "" if pd.isna(r["pct_change"]) else f"{num(r['pct_change'], 0)}%"
    p = "<0.001" if r["p"] < 0.001 else f"{r['p']:.3f}"
    ph = "<0.001" if r["p_holm"] < 0.001 else f"{r['p_holm']:.3f}"
    verdict = "**significant**" if r["significant"] == True else "not significant"
    lines.append(f"| {r['test'].replace('_', ' ')} | {r['region']} | {ALT[r['alternative']]} | "
                 f"{num(r['estimate'], d)} | {num(r['ci_low'], d)} to {num(r['ci_high'], d)} | "
                 f"{change} | {p} | {ph} | {verdict} |")
print("\n".join(lines))
```

Units: H1 in mm of December to February precipitation, El Niño winters minus
the rest. H2 in log points of burned area, El Niño seasons minus the rest.
H3 and H4 in log points per 1 °C of the winter index. H5 and H6 in log
points per standard deviation of the predictor. C1 and C2 per year. The
p-value is in the registered direction.

## What was filtered out

- **Small fires.** Only fires of `{python} S["min_fire_ha"]` ha (1,000
  acres) or more count, in every region, because that is the size MTBS maps
  in the West. The floor applies to the whole fire before it is cut to a
  region. Regions where burned area comes mostly from smaller fires are
  undercounted.
- **Prescribed fire.** Dropped from all three sources.
- **Fires outside the season.** A fire counts by its ignition date:
  June to October in the Pacific Northwest, April to October in British
  Columbia and Alberta, April to September in Alaska and Yukon, and June to
  the following January in California.
- **Overlapping perimeters.** Counted once. Summing them had counted
  `{python} f"{round(mn('overlap_double_counted'), -3):,.0f}"` ha twice.
- **Glacier and permanent-snow cells.** Left out of the snowpack and SPEI
  means, where they would swamp the seasonal signal.
- **Snow stations.** Back-estimated and suspect values dropped; a site filed
  under two IDs counted once.
- **Seasons with no counted fire.** Kept as zero. There is
  `{python} n_zero`: `{python} zero_rows["region"].iloc[0]` in `{python} int(zero_rows["year"].iloc[0])`. The tests were repeated
  with it handled the other way.

## Limitations

### "El Niño years differ from the rest" (H1, H2)

**The sample is small.** The fire record holds `{python} n_nino_seasons` El
Niño seasons and `{python} n_strong_seasons` strong ones. A reader might
take "no difference found" as "no difference". The interval says otherwise:
for Alberta the H2 difference is `{python} est("H2", "AB")` log points, which
covers anything from `{python} f"{np.exp(h2_ab['ci_low']):.1f}"` to `{python} f"{np.exp(h2_ab['ci_high']):.1f}"` times the
area of other years. The strong-only comparisons
rest on `{python} n_strong_seasons` seasons and are exploratory.

**The answer depends on the index in one region.** In the Pacific Northwest
the H2 difference is `{python} est("H2", "PNW")` under
`{python} S["enso_index"]` and `{python} est("H2", "PNW", kind="oni_robustness")`
under `{python} S["enso_robustness_index"]`. The two indices class `{python} int(mn("enso_class_differs"))` of `{python} int(mn("enso_class_differs", col="n"))`
winters differently. Neither result is significant, but the sign is not
settled.

**Winter precipitation was seen before the freeze.** H1 is a check that the
data behave as the literature says, not a discovery.

### "El Niño strength drives burned area" (H3)

**A null result here is weak evidence.** British Columbia's H3a interval
runs from `{python} f"{num(pick('H3a', 'BC')['pct_low'], 0)}%"` to
`{python} f"{num(pick('H3a', 'BC')['pct_high'], 0)}%"` burned area per 1 °C.
That is compatible with no effect and with a large one. What the test rules
out is a strong, reliable link, not any link.

**The index adds nothing to prediction.** Against a model with the year
trend alone, adding the index changes out-of-sample skill by
`{python} num(h3a_skill.min(), 3)` to `{python} num(h3a_skill.max(), 3)`
across the seven regions. Zero means no better than the trend.

**The trend term stands in for everything that changed.** Warming, fuel
build-up, suppression policy, land use and how fires are mapped are all
folded into one straight line per region. If any of them moved in step with
El Niño winters by chance, the model cannot tell.

**The robust tests run slightly hot.** On simulated data with no effect,
these tests reject between `{python} f"{100 * sizes.min():.1f}"`% and
`{python} f"{100 * sizes.max():.1f}"`% of the time where 5% would be exact.
The measured rate is printed beside each result in the results tables. It
makes a borderline p-value a little less convincing; it does not touch the
nulls.

### "The north responds differently from California" (H4)

**The two sides are measured differently.** US burned area comes from
satellite mapping and incident perimeters, Canadian burned area from agency
polygons. Where MTBS and WFIGS both hold a fire, WFIGS area is a median
`{python} mn_range("wfigs_over_mtbs_median")` of MTBS's. For Canada I compared CNFDB with a second national
product (NBAC): `{python} mn_range("nbac_missing_share", 1, pct=True)` of NBAC's burned area sits in fires CNFDB does
not hold at all. I did not rerun the tests on NBAC; I report the gap.

**Known holes in the Canadian record.** CNFDB holds no national-park fire
of counted size in these regions for `{python} park_gap_years`, which matters for
Alberta in 2016 to 2019 (Wood Buffalo).
The tests were repeated with the park area added from NBAC: Alberta's H3a
slope is `{python} est("H3a", "AB", kind="parks_nbac")` against
`{python} est("H3a", "AB")`. Fires on two military bases in Alberta are in
no year of the record: about `{python} f"{mn('defence_land_share', 'AB'):.0f}"`% of the province's counted burned area.

**Different end years.** The pooled model stops at
`{python} S["pooled_last_year"]` for all five regions so that the Canadian
and US series cover the same seasons.

### "Wet years set up later fires" (H5, H6)

**A lagged association is evidence for the mechanism, not proof of it.** A
wet winter is followed by more burned area in Northern California a year on.
Grass growth is one explanation. I measured the rain and the burned area,
not the grass.

**The effect appeared where I did not predict it.** I registered the
next-year effect as strongest in Southern California. It is
`{python} est("H5_lag1", "SoCal")` there and
`{python} est("H5_lag1", "NorCal")` in Northern California. A result in an
unpredicted place deserves more caution, not less.

**Large families cost power.** H5 holds `{python} int(fam["H5"])` tests and H6 `{python} int(fam["H6"])`, so the Holm
bar is high. Northern California's same-year slope
(p `{python} pv("H5_lag0", "NorCal")`) and Alberta's snowpack slope
(p `{python} pv("H6_swe", "AB")`) fail it. That was the registered price of
testing every region; I am not revisiting it.

**The snowpack is a model's.** ERA5-Land snow is not measured snow. Against
snow stations the regional series correlate at `{python} mn_range("station_correlation_z")`. Repeating H6
on the station index gives
`{python} est("H6_swe", "PNW", kind="station_z")` in the Pacific Northwest
against `{python} est("H6_swe", "PNW")` from ERA5-Land. Stations sit high,
and in the Pacific Northwest the El Niño snow loss is at low elevations.

**Alberta's snowpack slope moves with the fire rules.** Under the fire
rules as first frozen it is `{python} est("H6_swe", "AB", kind="frozen_rules")`
against `{python} est("H6_swe", "AB")` in the main run. The sign holds; the
size does not.

**Region averages include places that rarely burn.** Alaska's winter
precipitation averages in a wet coast far from the interior fires. In the
interior alone, winter precipitation tracks the statewide series at a
correlation of `{python} f"{mn('interior_alaska_correlation', 'precip_djf_mm'):.2f}"`, and temperature at `{python} f"{mn('interior_alaska_correlation', 'temp_jja'):.2f}"`.

### "The 2027 forecast"

<!-- D96, item 2 of 3. Approved by the owner 2026-10-13, with the "not for"
     sentence moved up. The two links were opened on 2026-10-13 (both
     load); the owner is to confirm they are the pages meant. -->

**Who this forecast is for.** I am publishing it so that a claim made in
advance can be checked against the season. It is not for deciding where
crews go, whether to leave, or what to insure. For those, use the seasonal
outlooks from the
[National Interagency Fire Center](https://www.nifc.gov/nicc/predictive-services/outlooks)
and [Natural Resources Canada](https://cwfis.cfs.nrcan.gc.ca/en/forecast),
which draw on fuels, weather forecasts and people on the ground. It is for
readers who want to see how much a winter can tell us, and so far the
answer is: not much. The analysis and its errors are mine; the agencies
whose data I used did not review it.

**The registered forecast model has shown no skill.** The plan says the
2027 forecast comes from the H3a model. On past seasons that model did no
better than the trend alone (above). Its
`{python} S["prediction_level_pct"]`% intervals held the real value in
`{python} f"{100 * loyo.min():.0f}"`% to
`{python} f"{100 * loyo.max():.0f}"`% of seasons when one year was left out,
and in `{python} f"{100 * fwd_cov.min():.0f}"`% to
`{python} f"{100 * fwd_cov.max():.0f}"`% when fitted only on earlier
seasons. So the intervals hold up when one year is left out, can be too
narrow when the model only sees the past, and are wide either way: they
say little more than "a typical season, give or take".

**The snowpack model does slightly better.** Its skill against the trend
ranges from `{python} num(swe_skill.min(), 3)` to
`{python} num(swe_skill.max(), 3)`. That is small, and I saw it after the
results, so anything built on it would be exploratory.

**What would make the forecast wrong.** A winter outside the range of the
record; a summer that overrides the winter, as heat domes and lightning
outbreaks do; ignitions, which no winter variable carries. The drought
index is also sensitive to warmth in a way that may overstate dryness in a
warm, wet Southern California winter.

<!-- D96, item 3 of 3. Approved by the owner 2026-10-13, with the snow line
     reworded and the last line dropped (the section below says it). Each
     line gathers a limit stated above; none is new. -->

### Where coverage is thin

- **Strong El Niño seasons.** The fire record holds `{python} n_strong_seasons`. The
  1982-83 event falls before the record starts in `{python} S["fire_first_year"]`.
- **The Canadian regions.** Their record stops at `{python} ca_last`, one season
  short of the US regions, and misses national-park fires in
  `{python} park_gap_years` and two military bases in Alberta in every year.
- **Small fires.** Nothing under `{python} S["min_fire_ha"]` ha is counted, so regions
  where small fires add up are undercounted.
- **Wet coasts inside the averages.** Alaska's and British Columbia's
  climate means include places that rarely burn.
- **Snow.** The snowpack figures come from a model, not from measurements.
  The stations that check it sit high, above where the Pacific Northwest
  loses snow in an El Niño winter.

### What the whole analysis cannot say

- Burned area is not fire risk to people. It says nothing about where fires
  burn, how severe they are, or what they destroy.
- Seven large regions hide what happens within them.
- Everything here is association over about 42 seasons. Nothing shows that
  El Niño, or a dry winter, causes a given fire season.

## What a fuller version would add

- **La Niña.** The labels exist in every table; the tests here look only at
  El Niño.
- **A prediction model.** A first version exists: trained on every past
  year and scored only on years it has not seen, it beat a model with the
  year trend alone by a small margin. It was built after these results
  were seen, so it is exploratory and sits apart from the registered tests
  on this page. That work continues separately; the 2027 season is its
  first real test.
- **Finer regions**, starting with Interior Alaska and the dry interior of
  British Columbia, so that the climate average matches where fires burn.
- **Climate projections** for whether the winter signal is changing; the
  historical tests for that (C1, C2) were too short to say.
- **The check that matters:** the 2027 season itself, compared with what
  this page said in advance.

```{=html}
(function () {
  document.querySelectorAll("main table").forEach(function (table) {

    box.className = "table-scroll";
    box.tabIndex = 0;
    box.setAttribute("role", "region");

    box.appendChild(table);
  });
  var sections = Array.prototype.slice.call(document.querySelectorAll("main section.level2"));
  if (!sections.length) return;

    section.classList.toggle("folded", !open);
    section.querySelector(".fold-toggle").setAttribute("aria-expanded", open ? "true" : "false");
  }
  sections.forEach(function (section) {
    var heading = section.querySelector("h2");
    var body = document.createElement("div");
    body.className = "fold-body";
    while (heading.nextSibling) body.appendChild(heading.nextSibling);
    section.appendChild(body);
    var button = document.createElement("button");
    button.type = "button";
    button.className = "fold-toggle";
    button.setAttribute("aria-label", "Show or hide this section: " + heading.textContent.trim());
    heading.insertBefore(button, heading.firstChild);
    set(section, true);
    heading.addEventListener("click", function (e) {
      if (e.target.closest("a")) return;
      set(section, section.classList.contains("folded"));
    });
  });
  var bar = document.createElement("p");
  bar.className = "fold-all";
  [["Collapse all sections", false], ["Expand all sections", true]].forEach(function (item) {
    var b = document.createElement("button");
    b.type = "button";
    b.textContent = item[0];
    b.addEventListener("click", function () { sections.forEach(function (s) { set(s, item[1]); }); });
    bar.appendChild(b);
  });
  sections[0].parentNode.insertBefore(bar, sections[0]);
  function reveal(scroll) {
    var id = decodeURIComponent(location.hash.slice(1));
    var target = id && document.getElementById(id);
    var section = target && target.closest("section.level2");
    if (section && section.classList.contains("folded")) {
      set(section, true);
      if (scroll) target.scrollIntoView();
    }
  }
  window.addEventListener("hashchange", function () { reveal(true); });
  document.addEventListener("click", function (e) {
    var a = e.target.closest("a[href^='#']");
    if (a) setTimeout(function () { reveal(true); }, 0);
  });
  reveal(true);
})();
</script>
```
